characterization_methods.key_findings: 19Al alloy aged at 650 °C for 3 h exhibits a Vickers hardness of 801.5 ± 20.3 HV.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: load of 9.8 N for 15 s; 5 repeated measurements per sample, averaged
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure Vickers hardness of the aged 19Al alloy to quantify the aging hardening response

interfaces.interface_notes: In ultra-hard Fe-Mn-Al-Cu alloys the new BCC and FCC Cu-rich phases form at the interfaces between β-Mn; the content of the FCC Cu-rich phase at the β-Mn interfaces decreases with increasing Al content. No TEM interface analysis is reported specifically for the 19Al 650 °C/3 h condition (TEM was performed on 15Al 600 °C/6 h and 17Al 575 °C/6 h).
interfaces.phase_evolution: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Ingots with nominal composition Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu (at.%) produced by melting raw materials of high purity (>99.9 %) in a vacuum induction furnace under argon.
Hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm.
Plates cut into 10 × 5 × 2 mm3 samples using electrical discharge machining for Vickers hardness measurements and microstructure characterizations.
Solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under argon atmosphere, followed by oil quenching.
Aged at 650 °C for 3 h followed by water quenching; this is the terminal state of this sample.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Vickers hardness measured with a load of 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample tested 5 times and averaged.

structures.overall_structure: The solution-treated 19Al (Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu) alloy is single-phase α (BCC). After aging at 650 °C for 3 h the α matrix has almost completely transformed into β-Mn; the paper states that at temperatures of 600 °C and above the α→β-Mn transformation in the 19Al (and 17Al) alloy is nearly complete after just 1 h of aging. Fine BCC and FCC Cu-rich precipitates form within/among the β-Mn in these ultra-hard Fe-Mn-Al-Cu alloys.

unmapped_findings: The elastic modulus of the 19Al alloy (181 GPa, measured through compressive stress-strain curves) and its fracture toughness KIC (3.5 MPa·m^1/2, from an average crack length of 35 μm) reported in the paper correspond to the HARDEST 19Al sample (peak hardness 917.8 HV, obtained at 600 °C / 10 h), not to this 650 °C / 3 h sample (b0021, b0023, b0061).

The β-Mn intrinsic hardness of the 19Al alloy (12.5 ± 0.4 GPa by nanoindentation) and its β-Mn Al content (17.5 at.% by SEM-EDS) were measured on the hardest 19Al sample, not on this 650 °C / 3 h condition (b0060, figure_014).
The ultra-high specific hardness of 141 HV·cm3/g and the maximum attributed to Fe-35.2Mn-15Al-5.2Cu belongs to the 15Al alloy, not the 19Al alloy (b0008, b0077).
The volume fraction of FCC Cu-rich and BCC precipitates reported for the 19Al alloy (6.5%, hardness 810.9 HV) corresponds to aging at 650 °C for 6 h, not to the 650 °C / 3 h condition (b0069).

No EBSD, SEM, XRD or TEM data are reported specifically for the 19Al alloy aged at 650 °C for 3 h; the closest 19Al characterizations are the EBSD maps at 525 °C/10 h, 600 °C/3 h and 650 °C/6 h (figure_006), the SE image series (figure_009) and XRD of 19Al 550 °C/6 h (figure_010).

The 19Al alloy achieved hardness values ranging from 263.8 HV to 917.8 HV across its aging conditions, with the peak reached at 600 °C (b0037, b0060); the optimal aging temperature window for ultra-high hardness of the 19Al alloy is 575-625 °C (b0038).
